speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As Members know, it will lapse after five years unless extended.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The first comprised mainly young Indian gang members, most of them in their teens to the 20s, led by a headman in his 30s.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They carried out armed attacks against rival gang members.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They also attacked a fellow gang member as punishment for leaving the gang.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Then, the headman called up all the others and said, "If any of you dare to leave the gang, the same thing will happen to you.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You will be attacked as well." The Police got on to the case.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The members did not want to testify against the headman and CLTPA was used.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They were prepared to give evidence; they were prepared to testify but they did not want to do so in public.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They feared as to what would happen to them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The second gang comprised Chinese males in their mid-20s to 30s.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many of them had antecedents for very serious criminal offences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They attacked others, used weapons to settle their disputes.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Again, in both cases, the victims were unwilling or unable to identify the attackers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The gang members were prepared to give evidence but not in Court, for fear of reprisals.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And really, without CLTPA, it would have been difficult to deal with the gangsters.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, that is, if you look at gangsters.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We also used the CLTPA again in the context of drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Often, because they fear attacks on them and their families, the couriers will not want or refuse to testify in Court.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And if we let that situation develop, it will affect our ability to deal with the leaders of the drug syndicates.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And that is the approach that is taken.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will just show two slides to Members.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we want to retain the CLTPA as a tool of final resort, if necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is useful to give Members a picture of the total number of detainees, not just for drugs but the total number.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, the approach is, where we can, we move to the criminal justice system and use CLTPA as sparingly as possible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have to tell the House, while the drug situation is under control, the challenges are significant and they remain.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have spoken at length over the last few years about drugs, the issues in the region, in the world and in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at the World Drug Report, for this region, if you look at the sources of methamphetamine in East Asia and Southeast Asia in 2015, East Asia and Southeast Asia were amongst the highest globally among regions and we have achieved an unwelcome record in that we have overtaken North America for the first time as a source.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Southeast Asia, together with East Asia, is also the second-highest source of opium.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, that is the nature of the problem that we face.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have shared with Members before that 50 million people passed through our airports.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to be very, very serious about the drug situation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the Misuse of Drugs Act is very effective.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we have this CLTPA as a backup.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The third situation that I would share with Members is the unlicensed moneylenders (UML).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: CLTPA has also been used against persons involved in loansharking activities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have been clear about that in this House.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It gave the Police broader powers to tackle the UML situation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We attack the UML situation from different aspects and that has resulted in, again, a drop in the number of DOs issued for UML.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If Members look at 2004 to 2010, on average, during that seven-year period, we issued about 20 DOs per year for UML.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If Members look at 2011 to 2017, that has dropped to about two per year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, we have used the Court processes to prosecute UML offenders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But again, there will be cases where the runners will refuse to testify against the kingpins.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The towkays, those higher up in the organisation, they operate behind the scenes, they do not have direct dealings with the debtors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2015, for example, the Police arrested the mastermind of a loansharking syndicate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many of the syndicate members were also arrested.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The main operators were based in Malaysia and Thailand.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They do so to avoid arrest and detection.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The lowest tier – the harassers, runners and bank account holders – they operate out of Singapore out of necessity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That syndicate alone was responsible for more than 600 cases of harassment since 2006.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members of Parliament (MPs) will know this; residents come to you.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These people who harass would set fire to the residents' doors, they lock them up – serious safety issues; they splash paint, they break flowerpots, they scribble graffiti and, of course, they deliver "hell notes" as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The whole idea is to frighten the debtor or whoever is in the house and, sometimes, it is somebody else who have moved in, and they frighten everyone around, innocent people as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, the syndicate members were unwilling to testify against the leader and other more senior members.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fourth, we also use the CLTPA sometimes to detain members of syndicates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The head made it known to his members that he would kill or harm any person who betrayed him and the syndicate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One person was, in fact, attacked on his orders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The syndicate members were quite unwilling to testify in Court against him.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But his criminal activities were dangerous, detrimental to our public safety, peace and good order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Unlike other countries, our physical size, smallness, also makes it difficult for us to relocate witnesses in such a way as to assure them and their families of their physical safety.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, given our local circumstances, our law enforcement agencies will not be able to totally satisfy witnesses that their concerns will not bear out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is a brief summary of the types of situations where we have used the CLTPA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Bill provides for the Minister to detain any person for a period not exceeding 12 months or place the person under a Police Supervision Order (PSO) for up to three years – we can it DOs and PSOs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This can be done if the Minister is satisfied that the person has been associated with activities of a criminal nature and it is necessary that the person be detained in the interest of public safety, peace and good order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court of Appeal accepted, in the Dan Tan case, and I quote, "section 30 of the CLTPA is similar to sections 8(1) and 10 of the Internal Security Act (ISA) in that power has been given to the Minister, to make the decision as to whether the detention would be in the interest of public safety, peace and good order." The Court of Appeal also said the phrase, I quote, "persons associated with activities of a criminal nature" is wider than persons who had committed a crime.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the current approach gives a degree of latitude to the Minister on what activities could be the subject of a DO.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Should we continue to leave it as it is?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or would it be better to list the type of criminal activities in a Schedule to the Act?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have decided that we should actually just list it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Clause 8 of the Bill inserts this Fourth Schedule.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The activities that are currently proposed to be listed have been either activities which have been previously dealt with under the Act or previously been mentioned in Parliament as being within the scope of the Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Activities relating to participation in or facilitation of activities for Organised Criminal Groups are also included.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The new Fourth Schedule will also set out the powers of the Minister in respect of DOs and PSOs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will list the types of criminal activity in relation to which the Minister can make DOs and PSOs under section 30 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, of course, section 30 sets out the fundamental requirements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In exercising the power, the Minister will thus have to be satisfied, which is the current position, that the facts satisfy the criteria set out in section 30.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In addition, it has to be criminal activities that are listed in the Schedule.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There seems to be some misunderstanding on the effect of this proposed clause.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There have been suggestions that this legislatively overrules the grounds for judicial review stated in Dan Tan.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Anyone who knows the law will know that that cannot be the case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This Bill allows for a DO or PSO on the Minister's orders, and it sets out the grounds and processes for making such an order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It sets out the rights of the detainee and the supervisee, including the right to have his detention or PSO reviewed or considered by an Advisory Committee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Minister has to be satisfied that the grounds for DO or PSO exist.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The application of the facts to the relevant orders, and whether the order should be made under the CLTPA, have always been for the Minister to decide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court of Appeal in Dan Tan pointed that out, accepted that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It said that Parliament may decide to entrust the power and the responsibility to make a decision to a particular decision-maker and, in the case of CLTPA, that is the Minister for Home Affairs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts are not to substitute their views of the facts or engage in the exercise of scrutinising the evidential basis of detention.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, these classic principles for judicial review have been set out in case law and have been applied for many years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My views on the applicability of judicial review are restricted to CLTPA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not proposing here to make general pronouncements on the applicability of judicial review to other legislation because different pieces of legislation have different wordings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My views and comments are directed towards the current Bill and the Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Clause 3 does not seek to affect the right of judicial review on the three well-established grounds Even if I did not say all these, it cannot, anyway.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Anybody who knows the law will know that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These principles were accepted in the Dan Tan case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court of Appeal accepted that under the Act, the Minister had the power and the responsibility to make decisions as to what the facts were, apply those facts to the relevant rules and considerations and exercise his discretion consequently.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court of Appeal also said that the scheme of the Act is such that the evidentiary basis for the detention is not scrutinised by the Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Third, as long as the detention is within the ambit of the legislation, the Court of Appeal accepted that the power to determine the factual basis for detention, as well as whether this is warranted in the circumstances, lay with the Executive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, the Courts retain the power to review the Minister's decisions under the Act based on the classic judicial review principles, and I have said what they are, the three grounds.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That continues to be the position; it is unchanged.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it crystallises the position as it stands now.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The third objective of these amendments is to set out in subsidiary legislation the obligations on a person subject to Police supervision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: By clause 4, we are seeking to make amendments relating to these persons who could be subject to PSOs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We want to remove them from the main Act and set them out in rules under section 49.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because these conditions need to be tailored to meet the needs of the specific individual.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is very difficult to have these in the main legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we put them in the conditions, to tailor it according to the needs of the individual persons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Clause 4 also states that a person subject to supervision – conditions are imposed on him but he cannot comply with them because he is in prison or he is under a Court order – then, obviously, he must be excused from having to comply with the conditions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Clause 5 repeals section 36 of the Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These restrictions will be set out under the rules to be made under section 49.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Next, let me move to the provision of powers to CNB.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Currently, CLTPA supervisees report to both the Police and CNB.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But where there are breaches of PSOs, the orders, only Police Officers have the powers to investigate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Clause 7 will now provide CNB officers with the powers to investigate breaches of PSOs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it is useful to consider Malaysia's experience.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2011, Malaysia repealed its "Emergency (Public Order and Crimes Prevention) Ordinance 1969".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This law allowed for preventive detention of criminals in the interest of public order, the suppression of violence and the prevention of crimes of violence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They repealed it and then they faced significant problems.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Malaysian Parliament then introduced the Prevention of Crime Act 2013, which reinstated preventive detention.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One of the Malaysian newspapers reported the Home Minister, Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, as saying the following in the Second Reading in 2013: "After the repeal of the Emergency Ordinance and Restricted Residence Act, 9,095 detainees from Simpang Renggam detention centre were released and assimilated with the society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This year alone, there were 109 shooting cases and all of them involved the secret societies." That just illustrates that there is usually a tradeoff.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We prefer not to give such powers to the Executive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then we must be clear-eyed about the tradeoffs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it is difficult to say one approach or the other clearly must be followed, but we must be clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Often, arguments proceed on the basis that we can have the current situation of law, order and security without any tradeoffs and yet we can do away with CLTPA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you must be prepared to face it after that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The tradeoff that the Government has taken, which Parliament has agreed for many years, is that we give these powers, we impose safeguards and we look at the situation every five years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, any proposal by the Police or CNB to detain a person under the Bill or to place him under Police supervision will be looked at carefully, by both senior officials in my Ministry, the Ministry of Home Affairs, as well as the Attorney-General's Chambers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The practice is that the Minister only issues a DO or a PSO after this process and upon considering the opinions of senior officials.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, the Minister must get the consent of the Public Prosecutor before making a DO or PSO.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It comprises prominent private citizens, including senior lawyers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have to scrutinise the investigations and documentary evidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The committee may examine detainees, supervisees, investigation officers (IOs), witnesses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They can also require further investigations of aspects of the case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Detainees and supervisees will have the opportunity to present their cases to the committee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The committee eventually makes their recommendations to the President, who may cancel or confirm the DO or SO.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In exercising the powers, the President may also vary the order but the President acts on the advice of the Cabinet.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fourth, DOs are reviewed annually by a different Advisory Committee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fifth, a different Advisory Committee yet again considers all cases of detention if they extend beyond 10 years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, cases where persons are detained for more than 10 years are specially scrutinised to understand why such a period of detention continues to be necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sixth, of course, as I mentioned earlier, the Government has to come to Parliament once every five years to renew the Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There have been calls in the past to make the Act permanent but we believe that the Act should be explicitly extended by Parliament every five years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, in addition to the legislative amendments proposed, I would like to inform the House of another development.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is something that I have been wanting for years and we are now doing it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Advisory Committee, as I mentioned above, is an essential safeguard for the system.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The ACs being chaired by sitting Judges will make the process more robust.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The CLTPA is a necessary tool for Singapore to dismantle criminal syndicates.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Secret societies continue to make up the majority of the detainee population.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is not surprising as strong loyalties and the pervasive network easily intimidate witnesses, making it impossible for an open Court trial.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Projecting into the next five years, the CLTPA still remains a necessary tool for law enforcers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is because there is still a need to be able to carry out actions even though witnesses are afraid to step forward and even when it is impossible to procure evidence without undermining the territorial integrity of another jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While international collaboration and technology, such as forensics and video recording evidence, may allow us to do what was previously not possible in terms of evidence gathering, technology has a flip side.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It also enables intimidation of witnesses and made it easier for crimes to take on a syndicated nature, multiplying the propensity of harm and intimidation like a sinister phalanx formation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This not a figment of imagination out of a comic strip.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, we need an arsenal of laws to deploy to deter and overcome the morphing nature of criminal syndicates.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I listened to what the Minister said quite carefully and I agree with the Minister's views that the fear of witnesses coming to Court does prejudice justice, does prejudice law enforcement and the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I agree with this because of my own experience.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When I started off in the Legal Service at the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC), when you know the suspect is very likely to have done it and the only witness to corroborate fears for his life or his family's life, then he does not come to Court.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Drugs under the Misuse of Drugs Act is a good example.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The trafficker or the suspected trafficker may have drugs but who is he trying to traffic to?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And, if the witness who is meant to have received the drugs so as to prove the trafficking case or the charge says "No, I don't want to come, I fear for my life and my safety", then it does prejudice the procedures.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Similarly, for the Prevention of Human Trafficking Act.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A person could have trafficked the woman, abused her and she is very likely to have been someone from overseas and, therefore, fears for the life of her family overseas.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What do we do with someone who, with all intelligence, shows very likely committed the crime but there is no witness to corroborate that?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Do we just let him go without the facility of the CLTPA detention?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, when I sat as a junior judge and there was not a witness to corroborate the charge, then the burden of proof is not met, notwithstanding a lot of evidence against the person who has been charged.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And, even in private practice now, having a good witness is a real advantage to the case.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, from my perspective, I agree with the Minister that when you have situations where all the other facts and all the other evidence point to the conclusion that the person very likely did it and you do not have somebody who is willing to come forward because of fear of his life or the legitimate fear of his family's life, we need something like the CLTPA to plug that gap.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Newspapers have reported some concern raised over clause 3 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, in my view, those concerns can be ameliorated as the clause does not change the law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Bill Supplement clearly says it is to "clarify" the law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What was reviewable in the past continues to be reviewable.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This promotes the rule of law as it delineates the parameters of the power clearly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is necessarily wide so as to not remove the efficaciousness of the Act but allows for a more concrete understanding of the scope of power and what is sufficiently serious – an issue examined by the Court of Appeal in the Tan Seet Eng case.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It recognises the problems with syndicates and also provides the possibility for international activities with local links to be tackled, such as that of match-fixing in the situation of Tan Seet Eng.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Nevertheless, it is important that this Act not be invoked merely because a criminal activity is specified in the list.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For the interests of justice, the Act should still only be resorted to, not only in the most serious of those activities, but when an open Court trial is impracticable.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A trial by the Court must still remain and continue to be the primary mechanism of law enforcement and judicial adjudication.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill also makes some changes to the Police supervisory regime.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One of them is regarding restrictions able to be imposed on a person under Police investigation or supervision.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Currently, section 33(1) allows for the possibility to impose "all or any" of the restrictions, and subsection (2) provides for the Minister being able to vary, cancel or add restrictions specified under section 33(1).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This seems to remove boundaries and categories on the kind of restrictions being imposed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As the previous structure also allows for some form of flexibility, would the Minister of Home Affairs kindly elaborate on the rationale behind this change?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, notwithstanding this Bill, it is important that channels of dialogue for amicable settlements of disputes between providers of essential services and their employees remain open and effective.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Insofar as CLTPA is concerned, the answer has been yes for reasons that have been enunciated in this House over many decades, albeit not without significant soul-searching and qualified support.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One important reason that underpins the qualified support for the CLTPA in Singapore through the decades has been the prospect of judicial review, which operates as an important safety valve to check against any excesses of the government of the day.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The importance of judicial review with regard to CLTPA was publicly expressed recently by the Court of Appeal judgment in the matter of the international match-fixer Tan Seet Eng or Dan Tan.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the outset, Mr Speaker, is an amendment to the Act even necessary?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To answer this question, it is helpful to look at what transpired in the aftermath of international match-fixer Dan Tan’s short-lived release under the CLTPA after the Court of Appeal ruled against the Government and in favour of Dan Tan.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Government critics focused on Dan Tan's re-arrest six days after the Minister cured the deficiencies in the original Grounds of Detention (GD) with a more detailed GD describing how Dan Tan’s activities had a direct relevance to public safety, peace and good order in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As stressed by the Court, that was the crux of the CLTPA – the Government had to show how Dan Tan's activities prejudiced public safety, peace and good order in Singapore, something it had not sufficiently done in its original GD.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, what was somewhat overlooked in the decision to re-arrest Dan Tan was the Minister's decision to revoke the DOs under CLTPA of three members of Dan Tan's global match-fixing syndicate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, the purpose of the Act and, more importantly, the separation of powers between the Executive and Judiciary as it currently stands, would appear to be operating effectively, giving the Minister enough leeway to take decisive action against individuals who, in his estimation, pose a threat to ensure public safety, peace and good order in Singapore, while being in a position to clarify and apply the Act lawfully even if it means revoking DOs in light of the clarification of laws by the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Quite simply, the system is working as it should.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In recent years, these include questions on the legality of whether or when elections ought to be called in a Single Member Constituency or a Group Representation Constituency, the constitutionality of section 377A with regard to homosexuals, the constitutionality of the Government's decision to extend a loan to the International Monetary Fund, a challenge by some Hindu adherents on the banning of musical instruments during Thaipusam, and the challenge by a Sikh prison counsellor on prison policy covering Sikh inmates, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In concert with a more educated population and a greater recognition of the critical role an independent Judiciary plays as a co-equal Organ alongside the Executive and Legislature, it is unsurprising that more Singaporeans are seeking the avenue afforded by judicial review for clarity on public law matters and for the Judiciary to have the final say on the legality of Government actions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would hazard that even the front bench recognises and agrees with the critical role the Judiciary plays as a feature of a good government and good governance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, a policy question or decision of the government of the day can only be overturned by the Courts on grounds of irrationality, illegality or impropriety, thresholds which are exceedingly high to begin with.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, the law covering judicial review has not stood still even if Singapore law does not recognise some of the newer heads and principles that define judicial review in the United Kingdom (UK), such as the proportionality principle, ostensibly because some of these new approaches risk substituting the Executive's decision for the Judiciary's, a concern which, in light of our separation of powers schema, is a legitimate one.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But even so, the Chief Justice, in his speech to the American Law Institute which I referred to earlier, found it appropriate to share the Singapore experience with regard to a new head of judicial review recognised under Singapore law – that of substantive legitimate expectation – which concerns Government action that is contrary to a promise or an expectation that it has created or encouraged.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For the man on the street and the average Singaporean, the knowledge of a continual evolution of the law on judicial review is a welcome development.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Justice must be seen to be done, and the evolution of the law on judicial review has required judges to make more, not less, enquiries on the facts and circumstances of a matter at hand so as to be able to decide whether the Government has made a lawful or unlawful decision.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At this juncture, it would be useful for me to recite a short paragraph of the Court of Appeal judgment in Tan Seet Eng which buttresses the point that even though the ambit of judicial review only covers the process and legality of how a decision is made, the role of the Courts is far from routine and administrative. "In our judgment, while it is one thing to say that the Court must not substitute its view as to the way in which the discretion that is vested in the Minister should be exercised, it is quite another to say that the Minister's exercise of discretion may not be scrutinised by the Court at all.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We asked (the Government’s lawyer) if he was contending that the function of the Court was confined to verifying, as a clerical matter, that the paperwork was in order and included at least a bare recitation by or on behalf of the Minister that formally complied with the statutory formula.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The (Government’s lawyer) said that was not his position and, in our judgment, rightly so.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We have already referred to the decision of this Court in Chng Suan Tze where an objective approach was laid down.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This plainly runs counter to any suggestion that the Court is confined to so narrow a role.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, this recognises that a Court may and, indeed, should examine whether the power that is vested in the Minister is being properly invoked." On clause 3 per se, the explanatory note to the Bill states that the Minister’s decision being final applies in any of these three instances: (a) that the person has been associated with activities of a criminal nature; (b) that it is necessary for a person to be detained in the interests of public safety, peace and good order; and (c) that it is necessary that a person be subject to the supervision of the Police.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More fundamentally, would it not be more propitious for Parliament to extend real scope to the Judiciary to review the Minister's decision in the case of CLTPA detentions, particularly since detainees cannot challenge the evidence against them in an open Court, notwithstanding the Executive check available by way of the Advisory Committee under the Act?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand the Minister spoke about the constitution of the Advisory Committee in his Second Reading speech and the idea of including judges as part of the Advisory Committee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just as a matter of clarification, does this not conflate the role of the Executive and the Judiciary?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would like the Minister's views on that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is a significant shift in the reach and ambit of CLTPA and I do have some questions in this regard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does the Minister have any examples of criminals having facilitated or participated in crimes overseas only for the Government to be bereft of any legal options to bring such individuals to justice?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More narrowly, would the detention of an individual arising from section 48(1) of the OCA under CLTPA require the Minister to include evidence or the results of investigations from a foreign counterpart in his GD or would some other standard apply and, if so, what would that standard be?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Or would it be up to the Minister, in step with the amendment proposed in clause 3 that his decision is final and there is, for all practical purposes, very little scope for any enquiry into this matter, if any at all?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Over the years, many Parliamentarians − backbenchers, Opposition MPs and Nominated MPs − have said in this House that the powers the CLTPA gives the Government to detain a suspect without trial may "nag" at their conscience.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I support, Mr Speaker, Sir, the hard choice that has ultimately, and always been made over the past few years, and multiple years actually, to revive the CLTPA.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: However, the amendment Bill before us today is different in certain respects.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to focus my speech just on clause 3.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I was originally concerned for two broad reasons.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: First, the amendment proposed in clause 3 could effectively liken CLTPA section 30 with section 8B(2) of ISA.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The ISA's 8B(2) expressly ousts "judicial review in any Court of any act done or decision made by the … Minister".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Judicial review, Mr Speaker, Sir, is an important check on a Minister’s administrative power in CLTPA and legislation as a whole.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Without the Court's review, there is fear that investigators, however skilled they may be, may make errors, that they might prefer to proceed under the CLTPA where there is insufficient evidence to sustain charges under a host of other statutes.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And Mr Speaker, Sir, I must say there are many.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: There is the OCA of 2015, the Misuse of Drugs Act, the Remote Gambling Act, the Common Gaming Houses Act, the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act, the Terrorism (Suppression of Financing) Act, just to name a few.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And, of course, there is the Penal Code.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: All these pieces of legislation, read together with the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC), allows for judicial supervision and due process, the hallmarks of the administration of criminal justice in Singapore.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, there was my concern that the judicial review process would have been removed from CLTPA by this clause.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It cannot be said, Mr Speaker, Sir, that the CLTPA's Criminal Law Advisory Committee can serve as a check on investigators' or the Minister's powers.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: After all, this particular body performs only an advisory function and has no decision-making powers of its own under CLTPA.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I appreciate, Mr Speaker, that the Minister has clarified that, as of March this year, there will be a sitting judge who sits as the Chair of this Advisory Committee.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But can I ask, for the purpose of clarification, whether the constitution of this committee and the purpose of this committee would change?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Would it be transformed into a decision-making body?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I do not suppose so, but I have that clarification.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Nor should the onerous task of being a check on investigators fall on the President who confirms DOs under section 31 of the CLTPA.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In these circumstances, what obligations can we expect to be imposed in due course on the Criminal Law Police Supervisees through subsidiary legislation?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Second, Mr Speaker, Sir, I was deeply concerned at first glance that history is repeating itself, when I first read the amendment Bill.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I was reminded of the Court of Appeal's decision in 1988 in Chng Suan Tze vs Public Prosecutor where a case was legislatively overruled.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I asked myself why should we wind the clock back 20 years to 1988?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Why reverse the Courts when the Minister just yesterday so convincingly reminded us of the need to trust the Court’s wisdom, regardless of whether we agree with the decision?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But if this is the case, may I just ask the Minister, Mr Speaker, Sir, as to why we are having the finality clause, or the words "final" to be included now, after all these years, within this statute?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If it is not to reverse Dan Tan or other similar cases, why should we do so now?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If the decision, as we know from the Court of Appeal case in Dan Tan, has always been for the Minister to decide, is it necessary to ensure that that decision is final in statute?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Having the words, "it is final", why now?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The apex Court's reasoning in Dan Tan at paragraph 74 bears mention, Mr Speaker, and let me just read out the most important sentences.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In the face of what the apex Court describes as a "potentially draconian power", I fear, and I would like some reassurance, as to whether the proposed amendments may ultimately have the effect of limiting the scope of judicial check on the Executive.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: As an example, on the of-chance if someone were to challenge a DO in Court, would the Court's role be confined to verifying almost as a clerical matter that the paper work is in order, that it includes a bare recitation by and on behalf of the Minister that his decision is such and, therefore, is final, and that he acts with the Public Prosecutor's consent?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I ask, how would the public, Mr Speaker, Sir, be assured that the GD without trial or continuous Police supervision in a particular case is not procedurally improper, illegal and/or irrational?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Given the Court of Appeal's reasoning, may I make one simple and humble recommendation?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister, as he reminded us even yesterday, is in a unique and special position, having been for many years a Senior Counsel and then a public servant.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Should we be mindful of future Ministers of Law who may not have the same set of skills, who may not have had the benefit of doing criminal defence litigation work or even representing people who have been detained without trial?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: So, looking forward, if there could be any safeguards which limit this, that would be perfect.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, it is available on the grounds that the Dan Tan case sets out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Third, I think Asst Prof Mohan would be aware, if you ask any half-decent constitutional lawyer, he will tell you that it is available, that such a clause does not oust judicial review.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am more than happy to confirm it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, judicial review, on the grounds they have set, they are not clerks looking at our records, they are judges, and they are entitled to judicially review our decisions, and they have set out on what grounds.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I hope Members will be aware of this as they make their speeches, otherwise, we will be dealing with an issue, of judicial review, which is not the focus of these amendments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why is it necessary to set out that it is final?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is the current position; so, we set it out clearly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Minister's position will not be looked at by the Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I also should tell Members that, prior to me, the Minister was not a lawyer – and one of his complaints was that none of his three officeholders was a lawyer – Minister for Home Affairs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And yet, if you saw the charts on the number of detentions, a fair number of the trend took place during his tenure.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The most controversial and draconian aspect of this Act is the fact that this law puts people behind bars without the usual due process.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Like the ISA, it is a controversial exception to our legal justice system which usually requires every person to be charged, tried and convicted in Court before he can be detained in prison.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To take away someone's liberty like this is not something we should ever take lightly to.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under section 30, the Minister can also make an order for a person to be subject to this supervision of the Police for any period not exceeding three years if he is satisfied that it is still necessary.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should also not regard supervision order lightly as such orders impose restrictions on a person's movements and activities, and they impact on his work and liberty.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The time limits for detention and supervision should also be viewed from the perspective that each order can be renewed indefinitely.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many Members have also spoken in agreement with the Minister of the day on variously the rationale for extending the Act to deal with the concerned crimes of criminal groups of the day.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I read from Ministers' and MPs' speeches in the Hansard that these range from secret societies, gangsterism, drug trafficking, murders, extortion and protection rackets, to, in more recent years, money laundering, loan shark syndicates, organised crimes and global match-fixing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There was also mention of arguably activities which are traditionally not regarded as criminal, such as prevention of strikes and lockouts as well as communist domination.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My biggest concern with this Bill is with the proposed amendments in section 30.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The explanatory note to this Bill details three matters: (a) that a person has been associated with activities of a criminal nature; (b) that it is necessary for a person to be detained in the interest of public safety, peace and order; and (c) that it is necessary that a person be subject to the supervision of the Police.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are the applying criteria leading to the Minister making a decision to make a detention or supervision order.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am concerned that, if passed, the Minister's decision on these aspects of his order can no longer be challenged even if the Minister's decision exceeds the scope of his powers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In respect of the Minister's clarifications and his comments earlier, may I seek the Minister's clarification whether the amendment that the Government is seeking would bar the Courts from objectively reviewing the matters that the amendment wants to now declare the Minister's decision as final?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Until now, judicial review is available to detainees to challenge the Minister's order if, for example, the Minister had not acted in his scope of powers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An order can be scrutinised by the Courts if it is illegal, irrational or if there is procedural impropriety.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is confirmed again by the Court of Appeal case of Tan Seet Eng vs Attorney-General.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the Court of Appeal held in that case, the Courts' power for review is not to review the truth of the allegations of fact found in the grounds given for the detention, but to scrutinise the grounds given to justify the detention to see whether the Minister acted within the scope of his powers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, the normal course of dealing with the criminals will be by way of prosecution in Court and recourse to CLTPA will be in limited circumstances where normal legal processes could not be relied upon due to reprisals to witnesses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two, the Court listed certain specific types of crimes and stated that the offences must have the following unifying characteristics: threat of violence and reprisal to intimidate witnesses; detainees associated with criminal activities of a serious nature, not just any criminal activity; the offences must pose harm to public order in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Court of Appeal stated, by way of example, the activities of gangsters, secret societies and syndicated crime gangs involved in violent crimes all affect peace, safety and public order.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the Dan Tan case, the Court of Appeal allowed his appeal and quashed his DO under the Act.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Court held that the facts and activities provided in the grounds were not sufficiently serious to fall within the scope of the Act, and also that it was not clear whether the activity stated had a bearing on the public safety, peace and good order within Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Judicial review is an integral component of the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon said in his speech on the rule of law at the annual meeting of the American Law Institute in May 2016 when he commented on the Court's judgment in Dan Tan's case, and I quote, "Judicial review is the sharp edge that keeps the government action within the form and substance of the law".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is this sharp edge going to be taken away from the existing section 30 of CLTPA by our amendments today?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: New Zealand high court judge, Justice Matthew Palmer, in his speech touching on the rule of law and judicial review as the Kwa Geok Choo distinguished visitor at the National University of Singapore on 20 January 2016 said, "I consider that the availability of the law of judicial review to test the legality of exercises of public power is a direct manifestation of the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If a public body purports to exercise public power in a specific instance, those concerned with the exercise must be able to ask an independent body – the Courts – whether the exercise of public power accorded with law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If it did, no harm is done by testing the question and, indeed, public confidence in law and government is enhanced.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If an exercise of public power were not made according to law, then the rule of law requires that be addressed, as it is when any other decision-maker acts inconsistently with law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To leave the decision to the Executive branch, untested, is to leave the effective determination of the law – a judicial function – to the Executive." I agree with what Justice Palmer had said.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is the change in section 30 really necessary?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is it right or fair to dispose of such safeguards now?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After 13 renewals, is this not a step backward?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will leave this point on this note.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I next have a clarification for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I note that the Minister has told us earlier about the latest development that judges would be chairing the Advisory Committee.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I seem to recall that what the Minister has said may be different from his suggestion in Parliament in 1989.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under the present system, the advisory committee, with the judges as the chair, will still have to report to the Cabinet, which will advise the President.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is what I understand the present system is.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And, for ease of understanding, may I just quote the Minister's remarks in his speech in 1989, at the Second Reading of the renewal Bill then. "The ISA can be justified under our circumstances.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the CLTPA, there may be more questions, and it has to be accepted that we cannot ever eliminate crime.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can only control it within acceptable tolerable limits.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the Minister has to focus on that and tell the House whether, at the present stage, the situation is such that secret societies, gangsters, the original justification, continues to exist at the same level of seriousness which justifies powers of administrative detention.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If it does so, then I will still ask that the Minister consider one structural change to the existing provision.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is to ensure that CLTPA is not abused.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reason I say that is, if the Minister takes a reasonable view on the facts that a certain person poses a danger, then presumably, the Act can be worded such that the Courts can look at the facts, the reasons for the Minister's decision and then come down on the side of the Minister.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not to suggest that it has been abused but only to prevent CLTPA from being a convenient route where the Police do not have sufficient evidence against common criminals to prosecute them in Court and, therefore, use CLTPA.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He has to rely on the reports that are put up to him by his Police Force.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And the Police do not have the monopoly of virtue and morality more than any of us.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, that is an important point and that particular provision worries me." So, I would like to seek the Minister's clarification whether what the Minister has in mind, as he introduced a short while ago, is similar to what he had said in his speech in 1989.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But it seems to me to be slightly different.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And, if it is different, perhaps I would like the Minister to share with the House why does he not propose to the House that we go the whole hog to what he suggested in 1989.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I next move on to the suggestion for the reduction of reporting period to the Advisory Committee.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It seems like a long time for such a referral.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am sure that when an order is made by the Minister, the Public Prosecutor and the Police would have and should have already carried out proper investigation and inquiries to reach the conclusion that an order is necessary.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the paperwork should not need much more time after the order has been given.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As highlighted in the title of the Act itself, the provisions of the Act were meant to be temporary to address threats to public safety and order in Singapore as necessary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In 1955, this was to address threats posed by secret societies and gangsters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Since then, the nature of the threats has expanded and evolved to include criminal activities, such as drug trafficking, murder, gang rape, robbery with firearms, syndicated crime organisations, unlicensed moneylending and human trafficking.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These are all serious criminal activities that have been mentioned during the Second Reading of earlier amendment Bills to extend the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Whilst the extension of the Act continues to allow for preventive detention without trial, that concept itself nags my conscience, to use the words of Parliamentarians in the House before.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In light of the hard facts that the threat of such serious crimes continues to exist to seriously threaten our public order and safety in Singapore, I feel compelled to support this Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In arriving at this conclusion, I am aware that the statistics show that DOs are on the downtrend principally because the CLTPA is used as a matter of last resort.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My assessment though is that the current situation is reversible.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister's narration of how, just in 2017, two gangs were crippled using the CLTPA, is evidence of this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The elements that promote secret societies and gang-related crimes are far from being "licked".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Their roots are deeply embedded within our society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We also need to be mindful about the crime and drug environment just outside our borders, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my assessment, there is a danger that secret society activities and gang-related crimes in Singapore may proliferate in Singapore if we were to allow these exceptional measures to deal with such problems to expire at this point in time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For this reason, I support the extension of the Bill for another five years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The sunset clause in the Act is a safeguard to ensure periodic scrutiny by Parliament.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This allows Parliament to be apprised of the prevailing landscape, in particular, to consider the prevalence of serious crimes and weigh it against the need for public safety and order, so as to decide if the original justification and basis for the Act continue.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I recognise that the present Bill also seeks to make amendments to other provisions of the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: However, these other amendments may be dealt with separately within the five-year period the Act is in force, so that such amendments would not take away from the issue of whether there is a basis for Parliament to extend the operation of the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This was done before on several occasions in this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I seek further clarifications on the proposed amendments to section 30 of the Act and hon Members have spoken about this, in particular, the decision to make the Minister's decision final.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: On the issue of whether or not a person has been associated with activities of a criminal nature, I understand from the Minister's clarification that the proposed amendment was meant to, if I could use the word, "codify" the approach taken by the Court of Appeal in Tan Seet Eng, in that the Court recognised that the Minister is competent to determine whether a person's detention would be in the interests of public safety, peace and good order.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Is it also meant to "codify" the judicial review approach taken by the Court of Appeal, meaning to employ what is known as the traditional test of illegality, irrational or procedural impropriety on an objective plane?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: If so, would it not run the danger of the Court not being able to update its approach to judicial review of Executive action in the future as our society develops?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Another proposed amendment to section 30 is to define "activities of a criminal nature" to a list of activities specified in the Fourth Schedule.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This is a departure from the previously taken position opting not to specify a list of offences or criminal activities for which the Act would be deployed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I understand from the hon Minister that this is to promote clarity on what kind of activities are contemplated.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In specifying a list of "activities of a criminal nature", I am concerned that this would unduly tie down the Minister's hands.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As the then Second Minister for Home Affairs Mr S Iswaran said in this House in 2013, "criminal groups reorganise and rework themselves constantly" and "new forms of serious criminal activities evolve in a borderless world, assisted by advances in technology".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Recognising this, specifying a list of the type of criminal activities may instead inhibit our ability to keep pace with creative criminals and possibly dampen the deterrent effect of the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For example, it is very possible that illegal betting activities may entail activities of a sufficiently serious criminal nature to fall within the Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As has been said in this House on a number of occasions, and which has been distilled by the Court of Appeal in the Tan Seet Eng's case, the main unifying features for offences for which this Act was meant to apply are: first, they feature situations where witnesses fear to testify because of reprisal against them; second, they are of a sufficiently serious nature; and third, they pose a threat to the public order in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In this context, the amendment to restrict the type or categories of criminal activity may cause us to be less nimble in tackling the evolving types of criminal activities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I would be grateful for the Minister's clarification on this point.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I am heartened to note the Minister's confirmation that even in respect of the specified types of criminal activities listed in the proposed Fourth Schedule, the activities must still be one of sufficiently serious nature and involve issues concerning public safety, peace and good order of Singapore to fall within the ambit of section 30 to warrant detention.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This is important to ensure that the powers are used sparingly and only in exceptional cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It may act as a constraint but it is also clear and it is better.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the one hand, we know that Singaporeans want Singapore to be a safe place to live in for ourselves and our families.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, we are very mindful of the tradeoffs of giving the Government too much power to detain people without a fair trial as power can always be abused.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is all the more so when we are dealing with powers that deprive people of their liberty for years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: During the past renewals of this Act, the Workers' Party has accepted the uncomfortable compromise that this law entails on the Constitutional right to freedom.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My colleagues Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Dennis Tan have already set out grave concerns about the Bill's apparent curtailment of judicial oversight.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Past debates for renewals of this Act did not have such a long timeline.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The hon Member Mr Murali Pillai produced a table.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For my part, I did the counting from the Second Reading of the Bill, not the First Reading, which is in Mr Murali Pillai's chart.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And from my counting, the last debate for renewal was in November 2013, less than a year before its expiry date in October 2014.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The previous two renewals, in 2009 and 2004, were debated even closer to the expiry date – between one month and eight months of the Act's expiry.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Why is the timing of the renewal important?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is important because, at each renewal, Members are asked to consider the prevailing crime and order situation then, and to decide whether an extension of the Act is justified for another five years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government itself has refrained from making the Act permanent, which means that, at each renewal, Members must satisfy themselves that the Act is needed for the next five years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, Parliament is asked to assess that the circumstances justify the renewal of the Act, from October 2019 to October 2024.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Notwithstanding that the Minister earlier shared with the House on the crime situation both here and regionally, how do we know what the situation will be like towards the end of next year?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How will Parliament make a reasonable assessment of prevailing circumstances so far ahead of time?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Does this not make a mockery of the careful consideration Parliament is to exercise when assessing whether prevailing circumstances justify a renewal of this draconian law?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, I move on to the inclusion of the new Fourth Schedule.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 8 introduces a new Fourth Schedule to include a list of offences which the Minister can detain a person for.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In MHA's press release of 9 January, it is stated that the purpose of the new Fourth Schedule is to “restrict the powers of the Minister by clarifying the scope of criminal activities under the Act”.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But as I read the Bill, this is not true.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Why do I say that the Bill increases the Minister’s powers?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Yes, the current Act does not list which kinds of criminal activities would make a person liable to be detained.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But that does not mean that the Minister currently has carte blanche to detain anyone he pleases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the landmark decision of the Court of Appeal of Tan Seet Eng vs Attorney General   1 SLR 779 referred to earlier, the apex Court made it very clear that the Minister’s powers under the current Act are quite limited.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In Dan Tan's case, the Court of Appeal did a thorough examination of the origins and purposes of the Act and also scrutinised Parliamentary debates on past renewals of the Act.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Court then came to some important conclusions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, the judges concluded that the CLTPA did not cover all offences but only criminal activities where trials in Court could not proceed due to threats of harm against witnesses or their families.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, the criminal activity must pose harm to the public order within Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In Dan Tan’s case, the Court found that the GD alleged that he was the mastermind of a global soccer match-fixing syndicate, but the effect of his plans was felt in other countries and did not affect the public safety, peace and good order within Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, in the Minister's speech and interventions, he appeared to be somewhat watering down the effect of the Dan Tan judgment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But if I may be permitted to make my own assessment of the significance of the judgment, the Courts made it very clear that it had a duty to objectively assess whether the Minister's Statement of Facts is coherent and within the legal scope of the Act giving him those powers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Court stated very clearly that its role was not limited to applying a subjective test as to whether the Minister believes that he is making the correct DO, but it was much more than that.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Let us examine the effect of the inclusion of the new Fourth Schedule.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Schedule will likely short-circuit the assessment process of cases suitable for detention.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In other words, the inclusion of the Schedule may enable the Minister to bypass answering questions as to whether a case is “serious enough” to justify detention, or why it is not possible to prosecute these persons in Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Concerns have already been raised publicly by several lawyers and academics that the Bill potentially allows persons to be detained for alleged activities of a more minor nature, now that there is a list of defined activities in the Fourth Schedule.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Another striking feature of the activities listed in the new Schedule is item 9, participation in, or facilitating, any organised crime activity as defined in the OCA 2015.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What will this mean if the Bill is passed?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This will mean that the scope of the CLTPA will be expanded to cover activities that are done overseas or that may not pose a threat to the public order within Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier in the Minister's Second Reading speech, I noted that he was very careful to say the Schedule consisted of crimes or activities that have been previously mentioned in the House and it also brings in the OCA, which I take to mean he recognises that the inclusion of the OCA is something new, not discussed or contemplated by the previous discussions on the CLTPA.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These activities could take place completely in countries far away.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In addition, by referring to OCA in the CLPTA Schedule, the Government is importing into the CLTPA the concept of “serious crime” under OCA.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But the OCA considers to be “serious crime” a wide variety of offences, including many crimes that are fundamentally economic or financial in nature.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The list of such crimes includes Goods and Services Tax (GST) fraud, dealing in goods for which customs duty is not paid, illegal betting, computer misuse and infringements of copyright and trademarks.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Do such types of cases typically come up for DOs under CLTPA?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: By now linking the OCA to CLTPA, enabling criminal law detention for OCA cases, is the new Schedule not expanding the Minister’s powers under CLTPA?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Court of Appeal in Dan Tan’s case has pronounced that the CLTPA is only meant to protect the public safety, peace and good order within Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In effect, the Bill makes the Minister a global policeman, with no equal in the world.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is a position too arrogant for this House to support.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Other Members have raised their concerns about the clause.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I will only add a few points to the chorus of concern.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As my Workers' Party colleagues and other Members have said, the principles of judicial review are well-established.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When a Court is asked to review a Government decision, it will overturn the Government's decision only if it finds that the decision was illegal, irrational or procedurally improper.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Our judges are well aware that they are not Ministers and should not be the ones exercising executive discretion.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier in his speech, I believe the Minister clearly understands these principles.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, what is the justification for the Government to introduce clause 3?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Minister keeps saying and saying that it is not intended to change the legal position, it is meant to preserve judicial review.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But it is a tenet of interpretation that Parliament does not legislate in vain.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, if I heard Mr Christopher de Souza correctly, he attempted to suggest that clause 3 was merely meant to clarify the current position.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But if one looks at the Explanatory Statement to the Bill, it does not say as such.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Explanatory Statement to the Bill says that this Bill seeks to amend the CLTPA for the following purposes and the first purpose is to provide that the Minister’s decision would be final on these points.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If what the Minister is saying is correct, that is, clause 3 is not meant to change anything, then why introduce it at all?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Why not leave it as the status quo, instead of causing confusion and possible problems down the road about what this clause is meant to cover?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Instead of welcoming the Court's clarification, the Government comes to Parliament with this finality clause.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As MPs, it is important for us to pause and ask: what is the public interest here?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Does the public interest not demand that we defend rigorously the Courts' Constitutional duty to ensure that the Government acts lawfully?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And for more than 60 years, no Minister has come forward to ask for a finality clause on his DOs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As I mentioned earlier, I have my reservations about the timing of this Bill, as I believe that to renew the Act now to take effect in October next year is premature.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I am addressing this Bill from a layman's view, as someone who does feel uncomfortable with detention without trial.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In the 2017 and 2018 Rule of Law Index compiled by the World Justice Project, Singapore was ranked 13th globally for the Rule of Law, which I think is a good ranking on the state of our judicial system and how much we have upheld the principle of Rule of Law.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Today, we are here debating on this very difficult and important Bill, the extension of the operation of the CLTPA.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This provision, however, departs from two fundamental principles of the Rule of Law – the right to a fair trial and that individuals should be governed largely by the law and not by discretion.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is true that the crimes which the CLTPA seeks to prevent are no doubt serious and involves complex considerations.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But are there other options and measures that might be less intrusive than detention without trial, yet equally effective to address the problem which the CLTPA seeks to achieve?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
