text: Has the Government, before taking the decision to extend the operation of the CLTPA, considered these options?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Government share with the House what these options are and an evaluation of their strengths and weaknesses?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: While the threats which the CLTPA address involve a severe nature, it does not lead to an automatic conclusion that the only way to deal with these serious threats is by detaining individuals without trial.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is a policy choice that we make and one that requires robust justification backed by concrete evidence.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I note from the Minister's statement that the number of people detained under CLTPA has gone low.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: However, as its name suggests, this Bill was meant to be temporary.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: One of the justifications for the retention of this Bill is that there are difficulties with prosecuting those detained, as involved witnesses fear reprisals should they testify in Court.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This is a legitimate concern that must be addressed.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But it points to a larger discussion as to whether there is sufficient protection of witnesses in general under our laws rather than the continuing existence of the CLTPA.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There have been proposed amendments to the Evidence Act and the Criminal Procedure Code to enhance protection of witnesses recently.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The Cybersecurity Bill, which was passed yesterday in this same House, contains a provision to protect informants.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We should re-evaluate the necessity of the CLTPA in light of these new measures to protect witnesses and consider tweaking witness protection methods to better protect witnesses to offences which the CLTPA are applicable, rather than to continue relying on detaining individuals without trial as part of the overall security strategy.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: By further extending the CLTPA, I worry that it normalises and desensitises society to its extreme nature and further entrenches the necessity of the CLTPA.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: All in all, I hope we keep with the spirit of the CLTPA, which was originally set out only to be of a temporary nature meant to address a unique set of problems arising from a specific period of time.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: One of the amendments, clause 3, states that the Minister's decision to detain an individual or subject him to a supervisory order is final.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Many Members have talked about it, and the Minister has clarified.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: However, after going back and forth, I wonder if perhaps this particular change could be reworded or be removed to avoid any more misrepresentations, because we can hear that so many people, and they are all lawyers, who have been asking for clarifications and we do not want in future that it be misread.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Its constitutional duty in reviewing the legality of the acts of the Executive must be respected and protected by other branches of the Government.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Each time the approval from Parliament to extend the operation of CLTPA is sought, the question of the sufficiency of safeguard of this Bill remains in the forefront.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We have heard the Minister outlining the six steps of safeguarding.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This seems almost like a case of the Executive checking on itself.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, if and when the Cabinet’s advice contradicts that of the Advisory Committee, how does the President make her decision?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: What if the President is of the same view as the Advisory Committee, but different from that of the Cabinet, what would happen next?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Given that detention without trial involves a serious deprivation of one’s liberty, should there not be more oversight rather than less?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, the introduction of the Fourth Schedule to limit the types of offences which the CLTPA is applicable is an implicit recognition that all powers must have legal limits.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Consistent with the fundamental rule of law principle that all powers have legal limits, scrutiny of the Minister’s decision by another independent arm of the Government − the Judiciary − is an important check and balance.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I propose to take a break now and suspend the Sitting for 20 minutes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will take the Chair at 2.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, during the Second Reading debate in 2013 when the Act was last renewed, Minister S Iswaran provided the guarantee that “the Government will always make a rigorous case based on a thorough assessment of all circumstances and the criminal landscape each time we seek Parliament’s approval to extend the CLTPA”.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While I understand the continuing public order and security pressures that justify the exercise of these powers, we should never forget the extraordinary nature of the CLTPA and closely examine the grounds for the Act every time it comes up for renewal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My Facebook post seeking public feedback on the Bill has generated a fair bit of comments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These amendments clearly concern many Singaporeans and I would like to raise four points for clarification, many of which come directly from members of the public.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The first point was about the judicial review and I am glad that the Minister has clarified this in his speech.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That will allay a lot of the concerns on the ground.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the Advisory Committee.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If this has happened several times, my concern is that the objective of an independent advisory committee is undermined if a significant number of recommendations not to detain are ignored.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why might the decision be made against adopting recommendations of the Committee which would have made its recommendation after scrutinising the investigations and documentary evidence, hearing the detainees present their case, and examining the detainees, investigating officers and witnesses?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister provide some examples as to why a recommendation is not accepted?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Also, where its recommendations are not accepted, can reasons be publicly made for such a decision?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: During the last renewal of the CLTPA, Minister S Iswaran, and today Minister Shanmugan as well, had explained that the CLTPA is intended to complement the other legislation like the OCA and Misuse of Drugs Act by addressing situations where it is not possible to prosecute persons in Court because witnesses are fearful or unwilling to testify.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One suggestion put to me is whether the other legislation can be amended to address the difficulty in securing witness testimony in open Court.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Has the Ministry studied other solutions for addressing this problem which will lessen the need to rely on the powers under the CLTPA?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, the current sections 33 and 34 set out the restrictions on persons subject to a PSO.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill amendments will have the effect of moving these restrictions into subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many of these restrictions involve significant limitations on an individual’s personal liberty and freedom of movement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These include restrictions on place of residence, reporting requirements, restrictions on leaving Singapore and curfew requirements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The rationale provided is that this provides the Minister more flexibility to impose obligations and restrictions on criminal law Police supervision.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given how intrusive some of these measures may be, it would be more desirable for these restrictions to remain under the principal Act where it can be subject to legislative scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on the circumstances that have prompted the move of these restrictions into subsidiary legislation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Are there specific situations in which these powers have proven to be inadequate in providing supervision and what are some examples of further powers that may additionally be required?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, the new section 47(5A) will extend Police powers to investigate an arrestable offence under section 33(3) to CNB officers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As I raised during the Second Reading of the Immigration (Amendment) Bill last month, extending Police powers to Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) officers and now CNB officers are an expansion of Executive powers that should always be done cautiously.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify if these amendments were prompted by challenges faced by the Police in responding adequately to section 33(3) offences?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   The CLTPA should be, going by its name, a temporary one.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, in reality, the Act is not temporary at all.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Hence, many so-called human rights activists and organisations have called for repealing of the Act.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Just last week, I received one such email.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, I do not think we should be influenced by these human rights organisations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We should objectively study the benefits and shortcomings of this Act.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Detention without trial is not unique to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: After 9/11, the UK introduced the Anti-Terrorism, Crime and Security Act to allow the Government to arrest people who are suspected of international terrorism and to detain them indefinitely without trial or sentencing by the Court.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In fact, according to a 2014 study by the International Centre for Prison Studies, globally, there are as many as 2.5 million people who are detained without trial.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: There are more than 200 countries involved, including western countries, such as the United States (US), France, Denmark and Italy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In other words, the practice of detention without trial is not yet ready to be repealed completely at the moment.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I am not trying to put in good words for bad guys.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If the Act is still useful, we have the duty to provide certain safeguards for Singaporeans who are detained without trial.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: First, I would like to ask the Minister whether MHA has observed a trend that there are more and more people who are unwilling to come forward to testify in today’s Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Second, can MHA consider publishing the number of Singaporeans detained under the Act, the reason, the length of detention, and how many have been detained repeatedly.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Third, can MHA consider strengthening the power, influence and responsibility of the Advisory Committee and publish the names of the Committee Members to increase transparency?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In 2013, MHA kindly accepted my suggestion to publish the number of CLTPA detainees and the type of criminal activities the detainees were associated with on an annual basis.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The declining numbers reflect what former MHA Minister Wong Kan Seng said in 2009 that CLTPA is "only used as a last resort when a serious crime has been committed and a Court prosecution is not possible because witnesses are not willing or afraid to testify in Court." And a while ago, Minister Shanmugam has also given the same assurance.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Is MHA observing that more and more witnesses are not willing or afraid to testify in open Court?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: What are the additional principles that will guide MHA to decide when to prosecute the accused persons in open Court or dealt with under CLTPA?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Taking the example of the high-profile murder of Kim Jong Nam in Kuala Lumpur, would this be an instance when CLTPA would be used, rather than an open Court trial?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I also note that under section 28 of CLTPA, the Minister has the power to amend any schedule, and correct me if I am wrong, that the Minister also has the power to amend the new Fourth Schedule by notification in the Gazette without going through Parliament.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Does MHA have plans to amend the Fourth Schedule from time to time?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For better accountability, could the Minister consider providing an explanation and rationale as and when the Fourth Schedule is amended?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In my early days with the Singapore Police Force, I had investigated a gang rape case involving teenagers, which would today fall under the CLTPA if the Bill is passed.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: There were challenges in gathering evidence as some of the accused persons and witnesses went into hiding outside of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Eventually, the case was resolved and the culprits pleaded guilty in Court.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If they had been detained under CLTPA, the investigator would have an easier time, but it might have led to concerns by their parents and others over the lack of transparency.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Given the declining birth rate in Singapore, each child is getting more precious.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Hence, would the Minister be able to clarify why was CLTPA used against such youths rather than charging them in Court?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Do these youths have the means, influence and connection to intimidate the witnesses?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Of course, the Minister's decision to appoint a senior judge as the Chairman of the Advisory Committee would enhance the standing of the Advisory Committee.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Could the Minister elaborate more on the process of the hearing by the Advisory Committee?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If a detainee cannot afford to hire a lawyer to defend himself, would MHA consider assigning him a defending lawyer?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Yesterday, the Minister said that even a child rapist is entitled to his day in Court and to be defended.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: So, what more can we deny a CLTPA detainee a lawyer just because he could not afford to pay?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It is a pretty long period, given that the order is 12 months.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In order for Singaporeans to trust the CLTPA processes and legalities, it is important that Singaporeans are kept well-informed.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, it is necessary for us to reassure Singaporeans that safeguards are in place that the amended CLTPA is not abused.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (b) Does the Act and the extension of the same give the Minister for Home Affairs unfettered powers to detain a person?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: And (c) Does this amendment seek to extend the Minister’s powers further?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Such situations would continue to occur, as organised and syndicated crimes as well as occurrence of violent crimes continue to exist.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We need to be able to deal with such situations effectively to maintain public safety, peace and good order.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Although the legislation grants powers to the Minister, these powers are circumscribed by its provisions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The proposed amendments seek to define these powers further.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is relevant to note that the Court of Appeal, in the much-quoted Tan Seet Eng case, said that it did not accept that the CLTPA "has a loose or open-ended remit".

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This list would make it clear to members of the public the specific criminal activities that the CLTPA can be used for.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Act is an Executive regime and the Court of Appeal in the Tan Seet Eng case has held that Parliament can decide to entrust the power to the Minister to establish the facts of a case, apply those facts to the relevant rules and exercise his discretion accordingly.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The amendment puts in statutes the Common Law position which has been the position all along.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: What is important to re-emphasise is that the judicial review process is still available.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I, therefore, accept that there are safeguards in place to prevent unfettered use of these powers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The rationale provided was that it is necessary and relevant for the maintenance of public safety, peace and good order in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Various studies rank Singapore as one of the top, if not the top, city in the world for safety and security.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Economist's Safe Cities Index 2017 also mentioned that Singapore was ranked top for "infrastructure security" and "personal security", and overall second, behind Tokyo.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When ranked by population size, Singapore is ranked top among cities with five to 10 million population, ahead of Toronto and Hong Kong.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Interestingly, World Justice Project (WJP) Rule of Law Index 2016 also ranked Singapore first for "Order and Security" globally.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The question is whether we can maintain such a high level of security and safety without the extension.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Minister share instances in recent years where the powers provided under this Act had been proven necessary?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to know if there had been cases where those involved in the defined criminal activities had continued to be members of triads or secret societies and committed offences repeatedly after their release.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Minister would also address concerns that permitting indefinite detention without evidence in Court or proof of criminal responsibility can be subjected to abuse of power, as mentioned by other Members in the House.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Also mentioned by other Members, one area of concern is that the final decision lies in the hands of the Minister for Home Affairs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are suggestions that it would be better to leave the decision to the Courts.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a safeguard, every DO and PSO has to be reviewed by an independent Advisory Committee.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: After the Advisory Committee gives its recommendation, the Bill proposes that the President’s decision for the order depends upon the advice of the Cabinet.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That is why there are questions as to why the President cannot act upon the independent committee’s recommendation without the Cabinet.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps the Minister can provide clarification and share his views regarding these questions.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that they, too, received residents' appeals in the Meet-the-People sessions or house visits or whatever occasion that calls upon us to not wait until things happen for the Government to take action because it will be too late.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe the Members will not disagree on the good intentions of the Bill which has earned us the reputation as one of the safest cities in the world.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With adequate measures in place, all Members can agree or disagree on how to ensure and prevent abuse of power.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Once again, I call upon the House, do not wait for things to happen.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Ms Sylvia Lim had asked me what my view on clause 3 is.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This case impacts our debate on the Bill for two reasons.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: One, it sheds light on the implications of clause 3 that says the Minister's decision is final.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I have also said that newspapers have reported some concern raised over clause 3 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: However, this concern can be ameliorated as the clause does not change the law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The Bill supplement clearly says it is to "clarify" the law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It does not change the judicial review ability of such an order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, let me deal with the need for the Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh has cited several surveys which tell us that we are among near the top for the "safe cities" index in the world, and we are right at the top in terms of law and order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have shared with Members the findings of another survey.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun, Nominated MP, cited the Rule of Law index, pointed out and said we were ranked 13th globally.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But he left out the fact that, in that ranking, we were ranked first in the world for order and security; and fifth in the world for criminal justice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He says we can borrow legislation from the UK to replace CLTPA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The UK is ranked 21st in the world for order and security, and 11th for criminal justice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But let us not get carried away with these rankings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are not the gold standard, the Holy Grail, by which we should automatically judge ourselves.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are only indicative and, sometimes, some of the surveys, the methodologies are highly questionable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, in the end, we really have to use our commonsense, the facts, as we can see them, what is in front of our eyes, the lived reality in the UK, Singapore and other countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As Members, many of us, in fact, all of us, should be on the ground regularly, we know what our residents want, we know what they feel.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Will we be happy to have the same situation as the UK?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Metropolitan Police Commissioner has said the menace of knife crime caused by London street gangs is a "significant issue".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are dealing or trying to deal with problems that we have kept at bay.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if we look at America – people compare us sometimes – though you have got to look at city for city.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Thirty percent of Americans said they were afraid to walk alone at night in an area within a mile of where they live.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are not attributable to a specific factor or specific legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But really, we have to think of what works for us and think carefully before we try to cut and paste systems from other countries and, frankly, not be colonised in our thinking.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If something works well outside, sure, we should copy it and we do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we do not copy it simply because it is somewhere else without giving due consideration as to whether it has worked well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we need the self-confidence to ignore it when others shout loudly that they have the best systems in the world if the facts do not bear that out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In terms of the timing of extension, Mr Murali Pillai asked: why are we extending the Act now?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are making a number of amendments and I am taking the opportunity to also extend the life of the Act at the same time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Ms Sylvia Lim also asked this question.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is about four years and three months since the last debate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have explained why and I will explain why again.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are putting in more flexibility in terms of our PSOs, as I have explained.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You want to tailor the conditions imposed on individuals for rehabilitation, for counselling and so on, it cannot be or it is difficult to have it in the main legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, since we are making those amendments, we are seeking an extension by explaining it clearly in Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I agree, normally it should be nearer the renewal date, not right at the door but nearer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But since we are doing these other amendments, we are coming with a request for extension as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will now deal with three main issues that Members have brought up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, the finality clause; second the listing in the Schedule; and third, the safeguards in the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Several Members have spoken about the finality clause in the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked whether the finality clause was intended to exclude judicial review.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun worried that the amendments removed judicial oversight over the legality of the Minister's decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh also suggested we need independent Court oversight in the system.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Mr Pritam Singh, Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Dennis Tan also had questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In a criminal justice system, you have trials, you have verdict: guilty/not guilty.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For those who are guilty, the penal system provides for punishments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It works well because people know that if you commit an offence, you are likely to be picked up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you are guilty, you are likely to be found guilty in Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if you are found guilty, you will face penalties, and all of these will take place fairly quickly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The exceptions to this process – ISA, CLTPA and, of course, provisions in the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act (MRHA).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a deliberate decision by Parliament to make those exceptions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For the CLTPA, Ministers for Home Affairs have explained it regularly in this House and I have sought to do so earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The real world comprises gangsters, kingpins, UML attacks, threatening of witnesses, what I said here about the UK.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is from the Sydney Morning Herald, about an incident, it is just one indication, one incident, but it tells you what happens, and why we do not have such things in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is 30 January 2012, six years ago, an article: "The leader of Comanchero, an outlaw bikie gang, is refusing to cooperate with police after surviving another attempt on his life, a shooting that also killed his son.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Vincenzo Focarelli is in hospital with gunshot wounds, refusing to tell police who shot him and killed his son, Giovanni, 22, at Dry Creek in Adelaide Northwest last night.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was the fourth attempt on Vincenzo's life.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He was shot in the leg in December, was also the target of a failed bomb attack by two men linked to the Hells Angels, who both died when the device exploded early.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He reportedly taunted his rivals on Facebook a day after surviving the third attempt on his life, including boasting that he had nine lives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He can be seen dancing in a YouTube clip that appears to be promoting life in the Comanchero gang in Adelaide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Detective Superintendent Grant Moyle said, "Police will do everything they could to prevent retaliation", and this is after four times.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The detective superintendent was quoted as saying, "I would suggest it was a very planned, targeted attempt on his life", he told reporters that day at an overnight press conference. "It is a concern to us that retribution might take place, but we will do what we can to talk sense into these people.' " You can just imagine trying to talk sense into them. "He (Vincenzo) has declined to provide us any information that might assist us in identifying the offender.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is a difficulty we face in these particular cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The people that do know the information are often reluctant to assist the investigation".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, here you have a man who is publicly known as being part of a gang, whose life has been attempted on four times.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: His son has been killed, he is in hospital, he is refusing to talk.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The police feared that there will be retaliation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The police say, "We will try and prevent it".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we know in the real world what happens.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The article goes on: "South Australian Police Minister Jennifer Rankine will be briefed on the shooting by Police Commissioner.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She said police are doing their best to deal with the scourge of outlaw gangs and South Australia had very tough anti-bikie laws.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Hundreds of them have been arrested and charged.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Hundreds of their associates have been arrested and charged.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The frustration is these people have absolutely no regard for the law or, it would appear, for their safety or the safety of the community." The reporter points out that his son also had been attacked before but had refused to cooperate with police investigating the attempted murder.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, police then were going on a door-knocking exercise to try and get evidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We do not have these things for one simple reason.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not that we are automatically different but we have become different.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, this is the tradeoff I talked about.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is no right and wrong approach but you have to be very clear about what the tradeoffs are.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some Members might recall, I think it was 2010, seven years now, over a period of three weeks, a series of young boys went on a rampage, different groups.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think one was in Downtown East, a young man was knifed to death, gang attack.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then at Bukit Panjang the following week, there was another attack.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Three weeks in a row and people got upset, and they said "What is happening?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Otherwise, every MP will have to answer to your residents because our people value law and order and security very highly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And 93% of the people are not going to say in a survey they feel safe walking in their neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When paint gets splashed, MPs would have to face them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When their doors get padlocked, when their doors get set on fire, they will come to the MPs and demand that action be taken.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the Government has got to be able to respond.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, right or wrong, as I have been upfront about it, you can choose either path, as long as you are clear about the tradeoffs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Society, as a whole, must be prepared to accept the tradeoffs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have come to accept that the path we are taking is probably better for Singapore and for society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is possible to make grand statements about liberty and security if you do not have to deal with real world problems.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: President Obama, when he was candidate Obama, he thundered "Choice between liberty and security is a false choice", meaning you can both have security and a full set of rights, including due process for all in the Courts in all cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And he promised to close Guantanamo, signed an Executive Order in 2009 to close Gitmo, in fact.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But then the US was having trouble finding anyone else who was willing to take all these people in Gitmo.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prisoners there were indefinitely detained without charge; citizens from 49 nations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The President then tried to move them into centres in the United States; there was a big outcry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Senators did not want Gitmo closed and they certainly did not want these prisoners on US soil for all the rhetoric from the US.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Majority of the Americans also oppose bringing the detainees to American soil.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the President recognised the difficulty almost immediately after he took office.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, he said in a 2009 speech after he became President, "There remains the question of the Gitmo detainees who cannot be prosecuted and yet who pose a clear danger to the American people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I have to be honest here – this is the toughest single issue that we will face".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And he said, even after the process is complete, there will be some who cannot be prosecuted because there will be lack of evidence but who, nevertheless, will pose a threat to the security of the US.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And he said he is not going to release those individuals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at Eric Holder, the former Attorney-General of the US, he was giving evidence in Congress about one of the masterminds of 9/11.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He was asked what will happen if they tried the man and he was acquitted by the courts?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: His answer, "We would like the courts to convict him but if for some reason he is acquitted, we will detain him." Again, the reality of the situation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members know, for years, we have been lectured about the ISA, particularly by the Americans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But when they faced 9/11, suddenly the situation is different.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, CLTPA is not in the same league as ISA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is it better for society to leave them out, or have the CLTPA and use it?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our current approach has led to the current levels of safety and security.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Safeguards, I have mentioned several, including the Advisory Committees, the structure of how we proceed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, in this context, let us turn to clause 3.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have explained by reference to, first, logic, in that clause 3 deals with the factual basis for the Minister's decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, I have explained that a half-decent –and I do not mean it in an insulting way – my basic point is, any lawyer ought to know that, regardless of what I say, clause 3 cannot oust judicial review.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I have explained it and I have given reasons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am faced with an assertion from Mr Pritam Singh; and this is the best I can deal with it, unless there are some reasons given to me as to why he thinks, or Ms Sylvia Lim thinks or anyone else thinks that this narrows the judiciary's role.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court of Appeal itself says – I have repeatedly made that point; I even read out to Members the various passages – they made the points quite carefully.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They set out the grounds for judicial review and we accept it, and nothing here affects those grounds.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Hansard can be referred to in Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I am saying that as a Law Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, I say it as a matter of law, people will know it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Third, the Court also said they will accept the Minister's decision on the facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is intended to be the structure of the CLTPA, and that is the right approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You cannot go and appeal to somebody else and say, "Minister made these decisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can judicially review it on the grounds for judicial review.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is all in the Court of Appeal judgment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is, and has always been, the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked whether the Courts can go behind the Minister's decision and review the background facts behind the decision for the DO.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts are not to substitute their views on the facts for the Minister's views.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Read the Court of Appeal's judgment in Dan Tan.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As Mr Christopher de Souza and Ms Rahayu Mahzam have pointed out, the amendments are in line with the Court of Appeal’s decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai had some questions on the judicial review point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have explained the approach, the philosophy behind the CLTPA, and that the facts are for the Minister to decide upon.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On safeguards, Mr Louis Ng asked for assurance that the amendments will not dilute the requirement that the Minister has to provide the full GD.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng, Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Mr Mahdev Mohan have asked about abuse of powers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have talked about the inbuilt procedural requirements, the parties involved and the processes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the end, when you have given such a power to the Executive, there is a concern that there is some scope for abuse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Philosophically, you can say I do not want to have those powers and I am prepared to take the tradeoffs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But you should decide by accepting that if you do not have the CLTPA, then your law and order situation will get worse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not possible to say, but it will get worse; and whether you are prepared to justify that and take that kind of society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Slyvia Lim asked whether having a list will reduce pressure on the Executive to explain and justify each decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not see how this will be so, and again, a misunderstanding.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The current requirements under the Act set out under section 30 what the GDs are.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, again, I scratch my head when people complain about the Schedule; those grounds remain.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Sylvia Lim had some points and I tried listening very carefully.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have to say I found the points a little difficult to follow.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What I got out of the points under here was that: it increases the powers of the Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think these statements are difficult to deal with because they have got to be backed by some reasoning and some logic.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I come back to this simple point: you have section 30.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court of Appeal pointed out it is not unlimited powers for the Minister; it is not open-ended, but it gives a level of discretion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: After the amendments, assuming they are made into law, what is the situation?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You continue to need to satisfy the requirements in section 30.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the detainee is no worse off, the Minister is no better off.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In addition, the Minister has got to show that it is listed in the Schedule.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think rhetoric has got to match reality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it is useful to read the clauses carefully before making speeches.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Previously, when there was no list, some Members rose up – at least one rose up – to say, "Why don't we have a list?" Now that we have a list, people say, "Why are we having a list?" Mr Ang Wei Neng asked how the list is drawn up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng asked for the rationale behind the organised crime offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The activities in the list include criminal activities that have previously been dealt with under the Act, as I have said, or which had been mentioned in Parliament as being within the scope of the Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Supposing the Minister lists shoplifting as an offence, and then, based on that, he goes and detains a 12-year-old on the basis that this is contrary to the safety and preservation of public order in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do you think that will pass muster on any judicial review?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, one has got to be sensible about these things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It would not pass muster an hour before the legislation is amended, and it would not pass muster after tomorrow.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We included organised crime but it does not mean everything in the organised crime comes within the CLTPA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we wanted to pre-emptively, decisively prevent organised criminal groups from establishing a foothold in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Christopher de Souza is correct to say that this recognises the problems associated with transnational criminal syndicates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked whether the Act will be used against foreigners who dabble in organised criminal activities that have an effect in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That does not depend on the person's nationality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, action can be taken against foreigners, if the conditions are met.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Sylvia Lim says, again, in another rhetorical flourish, I will become a global policeman with the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it is useful for Members to read the Bill before they make speeches because we are dealing with serious matters involving the safety and security of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Not only must criminal activities fall within the list, a DO cannot be issued just because an offence under the OCA is disclosed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It must be brought back into Singapore in the sense that the Minister must find it necessary that the person is detained in the interest of public safety, peace and good order within Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not know where this global policeman comes, except perhaps it makes for good reading on a website where one can put out these things, sound bites, without reference to the legislation, the Bill or the clarifications.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If, and only if, the criminal activities, wherever conducted, impact within Singapore in the way set out in section 30, we should ask.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked what is the threshold of evidence for OCA crimes to fall under the CLTPA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The OCA does not provide for detention without trial.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It requires witnesses to give evidence in Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Where witnesses are not willing to do so for fear of reprisals, the CLTPA can be used as a last resort tool, provided section 30 is satisfied.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Mahdev Mohan, Mr Louis Ng and Mr Christopher de Souza asked about the PSO obligations and why we are moving the list of obligations to a subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The obligations, as I explained, you will want to look each supervisee and you will want to tailor the conditions according to the supervisee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some people may need counselling, just as an example, some people may need rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are conditions imposed on them to come back for urine tests and to be under general supervision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If it is in the main legislation, we will need to amend the Act each time we want to add conditions in, based on evolving needs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are all largely operational in nature and it makes sense to put them in the Schedule.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the extension of Police powers to CNB officers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Currently, both the Police and CNB supervise the supervisees but, as I explained earlier, only the Police have the power to investigate breaches of PSO obligations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The amendments will streamline the process, so that we would not need both the Police and CNB officers to be deployed to investigate breach of PSOs involving persons detained by CNB for drug trafficking.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng also asked if the Government will publish the names of the Advisory Committee members.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the members can choose to identify themselves if they wish, and some have done so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the Government respects some of the members' wishes not to have their identities published.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sometimes, they are also concerned about the people they have to deal with and what might happen to their families.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Mr Kok Heng Leun asked about the President's role.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The President acts on the advice of the Cabinet.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Kok Heng Leun also asked whether other legislation could be amended to address the difficulty in securing witness testimony in open Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The general approach, I have said, where we can, we want to move towards trials.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, these and other suggestions have been considered and are not workable, we have found, because the nature of the trial process is such that it is difficult to have a secret testimony from one witness who cannot be cross-examined and whom the judge can talk to but no one else can talk.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We pretty much have something similar now through the Advisory Committees.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng also spoke about persons under 21 who were detained and said each child was precious.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I wish to assure the Member that we only act when the risk of reprisals is there.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the persons detained are not quite innocent children.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They used deadly weapons, they recruit other members, they attack people and, in a way, you need to remove them from society so that other people of similar age are not influenced by them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is how you keep the problem under control.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If not possible, then use the criminal law, if it is necessary to do so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh wanted to know if there had been cases where those involved in criminal activities had contributed to the numbers of secret societies and whether they committed offences repeatedly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan asked about the Constitution and the task of the Independent Advisory Committee (IAC), and do they change by reason of these amendments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And they do not change by reason of the appointment of judges.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the past, our approach had been to appoint a very senior lawyer or retired judges.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I felt it would be good to appoint serving judges, but it does not change the nature of the Advisory Committee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do Members agree that in the current position, there cannot be an appeal against the Minister's decision on the facts?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court of Appeal has said you cannot appeal against the Minister's decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Minister's decision is not to be substituted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If that is so, then why do you disagree with the clause which sets that out?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, again, there has got to be some connection between rhetoric and reality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pritam Singh also asked whether having Judges sit on Advisory Committees conflates the roles of the Judges and that of the Executive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Judges sit as part of the Advisory Committee, they give their views, look at the evidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If they feel that some things need to be checked further, they can do so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They can call up the investigation officers, they can call for the files, they review these.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think we should welcome what the Government is doing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if Mr Pritam Singh or anybody else feels that we should not do so, I would like to hear that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Please stand up clearly and say, "No, we do not want Judges in there".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Say so and put it on record, if you mean what you say.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Separately, if the detainee feels that the grounds are not adequate and he wants to go for a judicial review, it is open for him to go for judicial review.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, of course, different Judges will hear that application, not the Judges who sat on the Advisory Committee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, having Judges who are independent adds considerably to the robustness of the process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Dennis Tan referred to my speeches in 1989.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I think he conflated the 1989 and 1994 speeches.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have not looked them up recently, but from my recollection, what we are proposing today to have Judges chair the Advisory Committees is similar to what I have suggested in, I believe, 1994.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think I made that suggestion in 1989; I stand corrected.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At the same time, I think I suggested some additional appointees to the Advisory Committee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Dennis Tan also said this is a step back.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would welcome him to clarify why he says that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How is any of this a step back?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, it is an assertion which is not being substantiated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am standing here and saying that this does not oust judicial review.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am saying any lawyer would know that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am referring to the judgments of the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am saying that the finality clause refers to the Minister's decisions on the facts, which the Court of Appeal acknowledged, and saying it is crystallising the current position.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Dennis Tan also made this suggestion ‒ this is quite a radical suggestion ‒ remove the role of the President, give it to the Courts to review.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Essentially, I think you need to be very clear about what is being suggested.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is the suggestion that then we do away with the CLTPA altogether?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because the Courts, as I told Members, is a trial process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a fundamental difference from the CLTPA process which is why I took some time to explain how CLTPA and ISA are processes which stand outside the usual trial process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, if you say substitute and bring the Courts back in, effectively, you are saying remove the CLTPA, just have the trial process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But that looks to me the suggestion which, philosophically, is very different.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Sylvia Lim made some other points on the finality and timing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Timing I have dealt with; finality I have dealt with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I have said, on the Schedule, I do not see how it increases the Minister's powers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng also asked about the process of hearing by the Advisory Committee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The persons issued with the orders will be informed of the GD.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will then appear before the Advisory Committee and could be legally represented.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Family members of the accused are informed by my Ministry on the outcome of the hearing once this process is carried out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I should add this in answer to Mr Pritam Singh's question as to whether there is a conflation of the roles of the Executive and the Judiciary in introducing sitting Judges to the Advisory Committee; I think Ms Sylvia Lim said this in 2013.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I am wrong, I will be corrected.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She made what was, in essence, a similar proposal that we have a sitting Judge review the merits of a DO in camera.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She said, "If I heard him correctly, he was actually suggesting that a current sitting Judge who was from the judicial branch actually be involved in the Advisory Committee which is also, in a way, what I suggested earlier, except that it was in relation to the Judge sitting alone.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng asked about the provision of legal counsel to detainees.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have pro bono services and the Ad Hoc Pro Bono Referral Scheme.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the Law Society Pro Bono Services Office will assess the case and arrange for pro bono legal representation as appropriate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Given that some of the Members appear to have proceeded on a completely erroneous set of assumptions of law, and perhaps a misreading of the Bill, I wonder if they will now change their position when it comes to voting.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will open the time for points of clarification.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In relation to clause 3, which introduces explicitly a finality clause into the Bill, the Minister keeps insisting over and over again that there is no change to the law, there is no intention to, he said, "oust" judicial view and so on and so forth.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But if the Government's intention is really to preserve matters as they are and, by that, I mean the extent of judicial review will remain the same as what it was in Dan Tan's case, why bother to legislate at all?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Why not leave things just as they are so that everyone is clear that there is no curtailment or even a slight limitation or a change in the scope of judicial review?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: That would be the simplest solution I think the Government should adopt.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The second clarification, and this in relation to the Schedule, again, the Minister is saying that everything still relates back to section 30.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In other words, we have a Schedule there but no matter which activity is being picked, the Minister will still have to be satisfied that section 30 is complied with.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In other words, the activity affects the peace, good order and so on in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But the fact is that the Fourth Schedule, by importing the OCA now, explicitly has an external focus, meaning that if you look at the OCA, section 48, it defines organised criminal activity to include activities that are primarily conducted overseas.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, this is where my "global policeman" phrase comes in.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In other words, the Minister can now look at activities done overseas and he would simply have to make a statement to say that he is concerned it will take root in Singapore and that would justify a DO under CLTPA now.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Once again, the same question will come up.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: If the concern of CLTPA remains the same, in other words, the primary rationale is to protect peace, safety and good order within Singapore, there is no need to make all these changes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The law already provides for the Minister to safeguard peace, safety and good order within Singapore under the current provisions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, it would be good if the Minister would clarify whether he is prepared to actually just go back to the status quo, ask for a renewal of the Act for five years, and then we can all support it because we all want Singapore to be a safe place.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The first point is that I kept insisting that there is no intent to "oust".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I made two points: first, as a matter of law, this clause cannot oust judicial review and I buttress it by saying that, go ask any lawyer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, and because I have been advised so, and I know so, and I want to be very open about it, I am prepared to stand up here and say so, as the Law Minister and Home Affairs Minister, that there is no intention to "oust", and this clause does not oust judicial review.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are tonnes of cases that will say that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why not just stay on with the current situation?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I am making an amendment on something else.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a difference between judicial review and a normal trial process or an appeal from the Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, to say, "I am worried that this is going to oust judicial review, so why are we making that amendment, I am worried that that amendment will oust judicial review." There has got to be a connection between the two.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am dealing with the Minister's decision on the facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I sign an order detaining a 12-year-old who stole a can of beer, and say I am satisfied that this is necessary for the safety and preservation of good order, public order and safety and security.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You think I can face any Court in Singapore and justify that?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You think I can rely on the finality clause?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It deals with the decision on the facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, to say that "I am worried that these consequences might develop and, therefore, please do not amend", it does not seem to me a very logical argument.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think I spent a fair bit of time explaining.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We require what is set out in section 30.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We got to satisfy the conditions of section 30 and its conjunctive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You got to show that it is also listed in the Fourth Schedule.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think whether you are a lawyer or not a lawyer, Members can understand that does not dilute the current position.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I have explained why I am doing it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I feel it is good to set it out clearly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Everyone is clear these are the offences, but you still got to satisfy section 30.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, come back to this example of OCA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If he wants to charge somebody or he wants to proceed to investigate and the Police wants to proceed to investigate, and then the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC) wants to charge, they have got to satisfy the elements set out in the OCA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Supposing we want to use the CLTPA, then you do not have to go and look at the elements of the OCA as such, but you got to show that section 30 is satisfied, that, in some way, it impacts on the good order, safety, public security in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Does the finality clause not close that off for the Courts?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, assuming you accept my point that judicial review, as set out in Dan Tan's case, is not impacted by the finality clause, I have tried to explain my logic a number of times.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As to whether our Courts would go down the route eventually of saying, we will substitute our views for any views the Executive may have and we will disregard all existing law as to whether they could go down that route, I would be very surprised if they go down that route.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if they did, I think the government of the day will have a duty to come back to Parliament and talk to Members and say, is this a way we want the structure between the Courts, Parliament and the Executive?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are things for discussions for another day.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But so far, as you will read in the judgments, due respect is given by the Courts for the Executive and Parliament, and Parliament gives due respect for the Courts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I do understand what the Minister is saying.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But the point is: in the case of judicial review, because the common law continually develops, is this the appropriate time for us to legislatively say, "Okay, this is where we are closing off certain matters in so far as the facts of the GD are concerned"?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If the judiciary moves judicial review along, should we not then come to Parliament, with the view, as the Minister suggested, to change the law even?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the question to ask is, are we comfortable with the current position, there is a right balance between Parliament and the Courts?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The framework of that, the appropriate balance, is today set out partly in the legislation, partly by decision of the Court of Appeal and previous decisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why we are putting it in law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we are not comfortable with that, I will be standing here, looking you in the eye, and saying we need to change it, as this Parliament did for the Internal Security Act.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Just now the Minister firstly suggested that I may have conflated his speeches between 1994 and 1989.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I have here downloaded from the Hansard, sitting date 4 August 1989.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said, I have not read them recently.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Because that suggestion seems rather unfair to me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: No, no, no, what I said is, I think I made the suggestion in 1994, but I heard you saying I said it in 1989.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not recall saying it in 1989, I thought I said it in 1994, but I will stand corrected.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The Minister went on to say that I made the, if I remember correctly, "radical" suggestion that the Courts, the judges should replace the Advisory Committee.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Actually, what I did as Members of the House may recall, is that I quoted from the Minister's speech in 1989, and if you were to bear with me, can I just read a small chunk of it here and it is very clear.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: And I will re-ask that question to the Minister again.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The Advisory Committee advises the President and the President has ultimate powers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I would suggest that the Minister still decide on the detention, but perhaps powers of review be given to the Courts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The reason I say that is if the Minister takes a reasonable view on the facts that a certain person poses a danger, then, presumably, the Act can be worded such that the Courts can look at the facts, the reasons for the Minister's decision, and then come down on the side of the Minister.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: If the Courts disagree, if the Judges disagree, then again the Minister's decision would be overturned.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: So, remove it from the President to the Executive and give the powers to the Courts." So, this is not my suggestion.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I do not wish to take the credit.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I asked the Minister because he brought up to the House that he has asked Judges to chair the Advisory Committee.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: And I recalled that the Minister had suggested this in 1989.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: So, I wanted to ask the Minister why did he stop short of not going towards what he had suggested in 1989, and instead he has asked the Judges to sit as chair of the Advisory Committee?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I was wondering which MP would refer to me and my speeches in 1989 and 1994.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But before we proceed, can I read this paragraph from the judgment of the Court of Appeal?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To suggest otherwise is to displace the choice that has been made by Parliament as to which branch of the Government is to be entrusted with the powers in question.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court's role in judicial review which engages the manner in which the power is exercised will then be limited to such things as illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This perspective is premised on a proper understanding of the role of the respective branches of Government, especially in this context of the Executive and the Judiciary in a democracy where the Constitution reigns supreme." There are many other points but I think that encapsulates what I have been trying to say.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not see how that is different from everything I have said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have the power of judicial review on those grounds.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But where it is within the province of the Executive, they will not intervene.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, as you see from other passages, they point out the decision on the facts it is for the Minister to make.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why clause 3 is worded the way it is, and which is why I was somewhat confused with the arguments on judicial review from both sides – some of the PAP Members as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I think it is good that we spoke about this because it helped me understand what the concerns were and helped me deal with it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I was coming to deal with one set of issues and suddenly a different set of questions were raised.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, Mr Dennis Tan, I think we were speaking at cross purposes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 1994, if I am not wrong, I suggested that the Advisory Committees have Judges but that is different from having a quasi-appeal process to the Judiciary which is in 1989.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you were referring to what I said in 1989.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I thought you were referring to what I said in 1994.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What we are doing now, in terms of having Judges sit in the Advisory Committee, is similar to what I suggested in 1994.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I misunderstood you because I thought you were referring to my suggestion today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, I think the Member asked the broader question.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The basic question is that I have said all these in 1989 when I was 30 years old.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why are we not going down that path today?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One can give a short answer, which is, I am 30 years older today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I believe in the essence of what I said then – in criminal cases, the usual process is to be tried in Court and that the ISA and the CLTPA formed exceptions for the usual process and, really, it is best if we do not have such exceptions or restrict those exceptions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Over the years, I also realised another point that was not very central to my thinking, either in 1989 or 1994, but a bit of time spent in practice and on the ground brought home the reality of tradeoffs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you are not dealing with people on the ground, dealing with day-to-day issues, one can get somewhat theoretical about these things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The law has got to work in a way where it delivers not just grand pronouncements, but actual results.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The question of tradeoffs was not something I factored very strongly in my thinking in 1989 and 1994.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I suspect that for a lot of people who approached these pieces of legislation, the assumption is that we see Singapore as it is today, this is how it will be even if you make all these changes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Supposing we remove the CLTPA, nothing will happen.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not saying that is your position, Mr Dennis Tan, but I am saying that, often, some of the people who approach these pieces of legislation approach it that way.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think you do and I do not think your fellow Members do because you have, in the past, supported the CLTPA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I am explaining my position, the question of tradeoffs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The assumption is that nothing will change in the real world and you can change around with the CLTPA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But in the real world, you have gangsters.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have read out to Members what happened in Sydney.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am sure that is the lived reality on a very much regular basis for a lot of people around cities around the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The kingpins are quite untouchable by the normal process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, question – and I make it plain in my first speech – you cannot say one route is right, one route wrong, but you can say there are these tradeoffs, are you willing to accept the tradeoffs?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The current situation of law and order that we have is based on the current legal framework and judicial and criminal legal system that we have.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if you remove the CLTPA or you tinker with it very substantially, you will get, I think, some tradeoffs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In terms of increased levels of criminal activity, whether they have increased, whether they will increase and how much they will increase by, that is something that one will only find out when you remove the legislation.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: Can I just ask two points of clarification which I think are important for both the Hansard and my understanding?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: First, it is a question I raised earlier in my speech but I just wanted to say it again.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: Where there is a judicial review proceeding under the CLTPA, will the written statement of the grounds upon which the Minister made the order – whether it is for supervision or for detention, and which is then referred to the Advisory Committee – as well as the Advisory Committee's report, be shared with the judicial review Court?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: I ask as this will be very useful for their review and I note that, in the Dan Tan case, it was not made available to the Court of Appeal at that point.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: My second point of clarification is: many of us know that the CLTPA is relevant and necessary, Mr Speaker, but why not make the amendments that are currently envisaged later when the CLTPA is typically and periodically reviewed nearer its expiry date?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the first point, is the Member asking whether we will hand over everything that was discussed over to the Courts?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan
text: To clarify, I am asking whether the written statement that is required under section 31 and given to the Advisory Committee – so, whether that written statement, as well as the Advisory Committee's report, will be given to them?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, the Minister also gets to see it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We felt that the discussions, the thinking of the Advisory Committee should be full and frank, and they should proceed as they wish.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If people believe that these things can later on be put up in Court and challenged, I think that affects the quality of the discussions and it affects the way in which people might write out the report as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is best that we keep the Advisory Committee as a process, put in good people, now put in Judges to chair them, let them look at it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The whole process is one where they can call for investigation officers (IOs) and if the IOs believe that this might ultimately end up in Court, whatever they say to the Advisory Committee, even with the best will in the world, everyone's behaviour might change.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At the same time, in Court, I have said what the tests are.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts finally have the power to subpoena documents, to ask for documents.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, if they believe that a certain document was necessary, it is within their power to tell the AGC to produce it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And to think that further, if we believe that the Courts are doing things in such a way that affects the fundamental structure of the CLTPA, then the government of the day will have to decide: is this acceptable, can we live with it, or do we have to come to Parliament and say we have to change that?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the Courts, as I have said, I do not believe they felt constrained, but they can ask both sides – counsel and the AGC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I cannot give Members a different answer from what I have already said to Mr Murali Pillai and Ms Sylvia Lim.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have been thinking about this for a while.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even though we take a very tough line on drugs, my thinking is, in terms of the first-timers, the second-timers, is there a way of looking at them not just as criminals, but in way that they are impacted by this and to rehabilitate them?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How can we get them back in the society?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we are putting in a lot of resources into the front-end in terms of preventing them from getting into the system, and then rehabilitating them, working with them, spending a lot of money on that in terms of trying to rehabilitate them when they are in prison, and then handholding them when they are out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you do not give them close attention – now, today, you make them report on a regular basis, that alone is not going to prevent them from getting back into bad company, going back into gangsterism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, my directions to the Ministry have been: can we do something more?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Can we tailor the changes such that the Police can impose certain conditions?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I can imagine you have to spend some time doing this; you have to come for counselling; you have to do these things; basically, it is to try and get you to break the habit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, that was the significant part of the change even though it has not been discussed today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
